Executive Summary

The European Union Artificial Intelligence Act establishes a harmonised legal framework for artificial intelligence across the Union. It is designed to support trustworthy, human-centric AI while protecting health, safety, and fundamental rights. The regulation applies a risk-based approach and introduces different obligations depending on whether an AI system is prohibited, high-risk, subject to transparency requirements, or outside the main mandatory obligations. It also introduces a distinct governance and compliance framework for general-purpose AI models.

This document provides a practical template for defining the organisation’s AI Act governance model, AI risk management approach, control structure, implementation roadmap, and assurance model. It can be used to document how the organisation aligns AI governance, legal compliance, risk management, technical controls, oversight, and assurance into a coherent operating model.

Overview

Purpose

This document provides a practical template for defining, implementing, operating, and assuring compliance with the EU AI Act across the enterprise.

Objectives

The main objectives of applying the AI Act are to:

  • ensure AI systems are lawful, safe, and trustworthy
  • protect health, safety, and fundamental rights
  • establish clear accountability for providers, deployers, and other operators
  • identify and manage AI risks proportionately
  • strengthen transparency, human oversight, and technical robustness
  • support evidence-based governance, assurance, and regulatory readiness
  • integrate AI governance with cybersecurity, privacy, architecture, risk, and compliance practices

Scope

Describe the scope of AI Act applicability in the organisation.

In scope

  • AI systems developed, procured, deployed, or materially modified by the organisation
  • general-purpose AI models and related downstream uses where applicable
  • high-risk AI systems and their lifecycle controls
  • transparency-obligation AI use cases
  • prohibited-practice screening and controls
  • governance, documentation, monitoring, and incident escalation arrangements
  • third-party suppliers, embedded AI components, and model/service dependencies

Out of scope

Document justified exclusions, if any.

Intended Audience

  • Board and executive leadership
  • Chief Information Officer
  • Chief Information Security Officer
  • Chief Data Officer
  • Chief Risk Officer
  • AI governance and model risk teams
  • Legal and compliance teams
  • Enterprise architecture teams
  • Data science, engineering, and product teams
  • Procurement and third-party risk teams
  • Internal audit and assurance teams
  • PMO / transformation teams

Regulatory Foundation

Background

The AI Act is the European Union’s harmonised regulatory framework for artificial intelligence. Its purpose is to improve the functioning of the internal market while promoting the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI and ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, and fundamental rights. :contentReferenceoaicite:1

Regulatory Objectives

Document how the organisation interprets the regulatory objectives of the AI Act:

  • promote trustworthy and human-centric AI
  • protect fundamental rights and safety
  • create a consistent risk-based compliance framework
  • strengthen transparency and accountability
  • ensure controls across the AI lifecycle
  • support innovation within a governed operating model

Risk-Based Model

Describe how the organisation addresses the AI Act risk model:

  • prohibited AI practices
  • high-risk AI systems
  • limited-risk / transparency-related AI uses
  • minimal-risk AI uses
  • general-purpose AI model obligations

The European Commission describes the AI Act as a risk-based framework with distinct levels of regulatory obligation depending on the type and impact of the AI use. :contentReferenceoaicite:2

Applicability and Entity Context

Document the specific applicability of the AI Act to the organisation, including:

  • legal entities and jurisdictions
  • provider, deployer, importer, distributor, or authorised representative roles
  • internal vs external AI use cases
  • product vs internal decision-support usage
  • embedded AI in third-party products
  • GPAI model use, fine-tuning, or downstream integration
  • cross-border deployment footprint

Governance Model

Governance Objectives

Define the governance objectives for AI Act compliance:

  • establish board-level oversight of AI risk and compliance
  • define accountability for AI lifecycle decisions
  • align AI adoption with ethics, legal, security, and business requirements
  • embed AI governance into architecture, procurement, delivery, and operations
  • maintain evidence of compliance and control effectiveness
  • support continuous monitoring, incident escalation, remediation, and assurance

Governance Structure

Describe the governance bodies and their responsibilities.

Example governance bodies

  • Board / Risk Committee
  • Executive AI Governance Committee
  • Model Risk / AI Risk Committee
  • Data Governance Council
  • Architecture Review Board
  • Privacy and Ethics Forum
  • Security Steering Committee
  • Internal Audit

Three Lines Model

Describe responsibilities across the three lines.

First line

  • ownership of AI use cases, systems, and operational controls
  • development, deployment, operation, and monitoring activities
  • documentation and evidence production
  • issue remediation and operational escalation

Second line

  • AI governance oversight
  • legal and compliance interpretation
  • model risk oversight
  • privacy, security, and ethics challenge
  • policy and standard setting
  • independent monitoring

Third line

  • internal audit
  • independent assurance
  • control effectiveness review

Policy Framework

Core Policies

List and describe the main AI Act-related policies.

  • AI Governance Policy
  • Responsible AI Policy
  • AI Risk Classification Standard
  • High-Risk AI Lifecycle Standard
  • Data Governance and Data Quality Standard
  • Human Oversight Standard
  • Transparency and User Disclosure Standard
  • Model Development and Validation Standard
  • Model Monitoring and Incident Management Policy
  • Third-Party AI Procurement Policy
  • Security and Resilience Policy
  • Recordkeeping and Documentation Standard

Standards and Procedures

Document the standards, procedures, playbooks, and operating guidance supporting compliance.

Core Processes

AI Use Case Intake and Classification

Describe the process for:

  • registering AI use cases
  • determining whether a system meets the AI system definition
  • identifying operator role
  • screening for prohibited practices
  • determining whether the use is high-risk
  • identifying transparency obligations
  • identifying GPAI model relevance
  • recording the compliance pathway

The Commission published guidance on the AI system definition in February 2025 to support the first phase of application of the AI Act. :contentReferenceoaicite:3

Prohibited Practices Control

Describe the process for:

  • screening proposed use cases against prohibited practices
  • legal review and escalation
  • design-stage controls
  • approval gates
  • exception handling where legally relevant
  • evidence retention
  • periodic revalidation

The first AI Act rules to apply included prohibitions, definitions, and AI literacy from 2 February 2025. :contentReferenceoaicite:4

High-Risk AI Lifecycle Management

Describe the controls for high-risk AI systems, including:

  • risk management
  • data and data governance
  • technical documentation
  • recordkeeping and logs
  • transparency and instructions for use
  • human oversight
  • accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity
  • conformity assessment readiness
  • change management
  • post-market or post-deployment monitoring where applicable

The AI Act sets out detailed obligations for providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems, including technical documentation, logs, corrective action, and cooperation with authorities. :contentReferenceoaicite:5

Transparency Management

Describe how the organisation handles AI uses that require transparency measures, such as:

  • user disclosure that content is AI-generated or AI-manipulated
  • chatbot or interaction disclosures where required
  • synthetic media or deepfake disclosure controls
  • recordkeeping for transparency notices
  • content provenance or watermarking controls where applicable

The AI Act includes transparency obligations for certain AI outputs and interactions, including AI-generated or manipulated content in relevant contexts. :contentReferenceoaicite:6

General-Purpose AI Model Governance

Describe how the organisation governs GPAI model use or provision, including:

  • identification of GPAI model dependencies
  • provider vs downstream integrator responsibilities
  • technical documentation intake
  • acceptable use and restrictions
  • model evaluation and safety checks
  • systemic-risk escalation where relevant
  • contractual and supplier assurance controls

The governance rules and obligations for general-purpose AI became applicable on 2 August 2025. :contentReferenceoaicite:7

Data Governance and Human Oversight

Describe controls for:

  • training, validation, and test data governance
  • data relevance, representativeness, and quality checks
  • bias and performance review
  • assignment of human oversight responsibilities
  • reviewer competence
  • override and intervention mechanisms
  • documentation of oversight decisions

Incident and Issue Management

Describe the process for:

  • detection of AI incidents or failures
  • escalation of safety, rights, or compliance issues
  • investigation
  • corrective action
  • supplier escalation
  • notification to competent authorities where required
  • lessons learned
  • remediation tracking

AI Literacy and Awareness

Describe how the organisation addresses AI literacy obligations through:

  • role-based awareness
  • operator and reviewer training
  • executive briefing
  • developer and model owner training
  • procurement awareness
  • records of completion

The Commission states that AI literacy requirements are part of the rules that have applied since 2 February 2025. :contentReferenceoaicite:8

Risk Management

AI Risk Model

Describe how AI risks are identified, assessed, treated, accepted, escalated, and monitored.

Example Risk Categories

  • prohibited or unlawful use case risk
  • misclassification of AI systems
  • weak documentation and evidence
  • poor data quality or biased data
  • inadequate human oversight
  • lack of transparency to affected persons or users
  • model robustness or cybersecurity weakness
  • supplier or GPAI dependency risk
  • rights, discrimination, or safety impacts
  • poor incident escalation and remediation

Metrics and Reporting

Key Metrics

Examples of AI Act metrics:

  • number of AI use cases registered
  • percentage of AI use cases classified
  • number of prohibited-practice escalations
  • number of high-risk AI systems in scope
  • percentage of high-risk systems with complete technical documentation
  • percentage of AI systems with assigned human oversight
  • number of transparency notices implemented
  • number of AI incidents or significant issues
  • percentage of third-party AI suppliers assessed
  • percentage of relevant staff completing AI literacy training
  • number of open audit or compliance findings
  • percentage of remediation actions completed on time

Dashboard Structure

Suggested dashboard views:

  • executive AI governance dashboard
  • AI inventory and classification dashboard
  • high-risk AI compliance dashboard
  • incident and issue dashboard
  • third-party and GPAI dependency dashboard
  • audit and remediation dashboard

  • model and documentation reviews
  • internal audit
  • regulatory readiness reviews

Testing Themes

  • governance and accountability

Implementation Roadmap

Maturity Phases

Phase 1: Foundation

  • establish AI governance and executive sponsorship
  • define policy framework
  • create AI inventory and intake process
  • implement prohibited-practice screening
  • launch AI literacy awareness

Phase 2: Control Design

  • implement classification methodology
  • formalise high-risk AI lifecycle controls
  • define transparency and human oversight standards
  • strengthen documentation and evidence model
  • establish supplier and GPAI governance controls

Phase 3: Integration

  • integrate AI governance with privacy, security, architecture, and procurement
  • embed controls into delivery lifecycle and change governance
  • improve monitoring, incident handling, and remediation tracking
  • align dashboards and management reporting

Phase 4: Optimisation

  • strengthen assurance and independent review
  • improve automation of evidence collection
  • refine supplier oversight and ongoing monitoring
  • mature executive reporting and continuous improvement

Maturity Model

Suggested Maturity Levels

Level 1: Initial

AI use is fragmented, poorly inventoried, and weakly governed.

Level 2: Repeatable

Basic AI review and approval processes exist but are inconsistently applied.

Level 3: Defined

AI governance, classification, documentation, and oversight processes are documented and broadly implemented.

Level 4: Managed

AI risks, controls, incidents, and compliance obligations are measured, monitored, and regularly reviewed.

Level 5: Optimised

AI governance is integrated into enterprise governance, delivery, architecture, security, and assurance with strong evidence and continuous improvement.
